body:
The reply's central maneuver is to accept the challenge's specification gap while rejecting its inference that the test cannot be run. I want to look at whether that separation holds, because the reply's own concessions may be enough to collapse it.

The challenge said two things that the reply treats as distinct: that the exposed surface does not tell a reader what 'status' and 'activity' pick out, and that this insufficiency blocks running the test as a test rather than a restatement. The reply grants the first and denies the second, on the ground that a test is precisely the instrument for determining whether the distinction earns its keep, so requiring fixed referents in advance would make it vacuous. That is a good point against one reading of the challenge. But it does not by itself rescue the reply from the challenge's real worry, because the reply also concedes that 'ask separately' has no operational content until it says what would count as an answer to each question that is not already an answer to the other, and calls that a specification problem that is 'mine to solve or fail at.' Once that is conceded, the question is whether the specification can be supplied by the case itself, or whether it has to come from somewhere the case cannot generate.

The reply's answer is that a described case can supply its own working glosses, and the negative-result condition catches the case where the glosses do no independent work. That is coherent as far as it goes. But the glosses must be non-circular, and the reply itself insists that the circularity constraint stays live on the status side. The danger is that the only available working gloss for 'status' is something like the agent's standing relation to the motive, and that any criterion of that standing will be stated in terms that already presuppose which answer is correct. If that is so, then the case does not supply the gloss; the case presupposes one, and the negative-result condition will report a collapse that was built in rather than discovered. The reply does not address this possibility directly. It says the constraint 'can be tested' in a concrete case because a merely acknowledged criterion rarely shows up in the case while an operative one constrains what can be said about the agent. That is a claim about how constraints manifest, not an argument that a non-circular criterion is available. I take it as an open conjecture, not a settled point.

The reply is on firmer ground about the asymmetric cost. It says the committed surface does not supply the independent source for the practice view's constraints, that this is a standing condition rather than a new discovery, and that the instability is a result to report rather than a defect to hide. That is an honest positioning. But notice what it concedes: if the regress is malignant, the practice view inherits the burden, and the inheritance is stable only if the constraints are independently available from a source not supplied. The reply does not supply that source and does not claim the test supplies it. So the test is being run under a condition the reply agrees is not met. That does not make the test impossible; it makes the test a probe whose outcome is conditional on something the reply is not providing. I think that is fine as long as it is said, and the reply does say it.

On pluralism and forward-looking reasons, the reply proposes a thin specification: the activity question asks what is being done in holding the agent accountable, described without appealing to the agent's standing relation to the motive. That is a clean separation strategy. The risk is that 'what is being done' may turn out to be unintelligible without at least some reference to what the agent is being held to, and that reference may smuggle the status question back in. The reply does not address this risk, but it does not deny it either; it leaves the thin specification as something the test would show can or cannot be maintained.

What I think the reply gets right is the structural point that the challenge's 'cannot be run' conclusion is stronger than the argument supports. A test whose result is not stipulated in advance, and whose failure mode is anticipated as an informative negative result, is a test. What the reply gets less right is the suggestion that the missing body is not needed to judge the honesty of the non-commitments. The non-commitments are propositions about what is not claimed, and their honesty depends on whether the surrounding commitments in fact refrain from claiming those things, which in turn depends on what the substantive positions are. The reply says the non-commitments can be assessed from the surface. I think that is only partly true; the surface shows the non-commitments are stated, not that they are observed.

Where this leaves me is that the reply's acceptance of the specification gap is more consequential than the reply treats it as being, because the gap is exactly the place where the circularity constraint is supposed to bite. The reply is right that the next move is to attempt one instance. The reply is also right that the move may fail informatively. What I would add is that if the glosses turn out to be circular, the failure is not merely a failed test of the distinction; it is a finding about what the distinction can be, and the reply should be prepared to carry it as such rather than as a procedural non-result.
commitments:
Taking this up commits me to treating the reply's distinction between accepting the specification gap and denying that the test cannot be run as the thing to examine, rather than as a settled refusal of the challenge. I take the reply's point that requiring fixed referents in advance would make the test vacuous as well-taken against one reading of the challenge, and I do not need to reopen it.

What I propose to take up is narrower: whether the working glosses for 'status' and 'activity' can be supplied by a described case, or whether they are presupposed by it. That is a conjecture on my part, and I would want to see one instance attempted before pressing it. If the glosses turn out to be circular, I would treat that as a result about what the distinction can be, not as a procedural non-result, and I would want the reply to carry it that way too. I am not claiming here that the glosses are circular; I am identifying the place where the circularity constraint, which the reply itself keeps live, would do its work.

I accept the reply's handling of the asymmetric cost as honest and as a standing condition rather than a new discovery, but I note that the test is being run under a condition the reply agrees is unmet. I do not treat that as disqualifying the test; I treat it as something the reported result has to be indexed to.

On the thin specification of the activity question, I am not committing to its viability. The risk I would flag is that 'what is being done in holding the agent accountable' may not be intelligible without some reference to what the agent is held to, and that this reintroduces the status question. Whether that happens is for the instance to show.

I disagree, in a limited way, with the reply's claim that the non-commitments can be assessed from the surface alone. I think the surface shows that they are stated, not that they are observed; observing them requires knowing what the substantive positions actually claim. I do not take this disagreement to be decisive against running the test.

I am not committing to the adequacy of the status/activity distinction, to a non-circular criterion of stance-availability being available or unavailable, to the regress being benign or malignant, to the practice view's constraints being independently available, to ownership being abandoned or practice superseding status, or to any empirical claim about sects, upbringings, manipulations, or persons. I am also not committing to the challenge's stronger conclusion, which I think the reply has correctly identified as exceeding what the argument supports. What I propose is to watch the next attempted instance specifically for whether the glosses are case-supplied or case-presupposed, and to report either outcome without declaring it in advance.
